slides.title: Why responsibility is the test of a legal order
slides.text: A legal subject is the holder of rights and obligations; violating an obligation triggers responsibility, that is legal consequences — sanctions in the sense of punishment, a duty to make reparation, or other duties such as abstaining from certain conduct. The slide then makes the point this whole course keeps returning to: responsibility is the test of a legal system's efficiency, because enforcement and effect require a centralised organ — and international law has only very basic approaches to that.

slides.title: Responsibility versus liability
slides.text: A distinction the English word 'responsibility' hides. RESPONSIBILITY means bearing the consequences of damage resulting from UNLAWFUL acts. LIABILITY means bearing the consequences of damage resulting from LAWFUL ones — the operation of a nuclear plant, the launch of a space object. Responsibility then divides by subject: state responsibility, responsibility of international organizations, and individual criminal responsibility. Liability produces civil consequences, often absolute, as under the Liability Convention in space law, and the liable party may be an individual or a state.

terms.def: Consequences of damage from an internationally wrongful act.
Consequences of damage from an act that is not unlawful — typically ultra-hazardous activities, and only under treaty.

cards.q: Distinguish responsibility from liability in international law.
cards.a: Responsibility attaches to damage caused by an internationally WRONGFUL act. Liability attaches to damage caused by a LAWFUL but hazardous activity and exists only where a treaty creates it.

slides.title: The character of state responsibility
slides.text: It arises from a violation of international obligations, is intergovernmental, and concerns the relationship between the injuring and the injured state. Its nature is NOT criminal but civil: purely compensatory, aimed at indemnity, bilateral, enforced primarily by the injured state, with only a few public-law aspects. And two simplifications worth remembering: it does not distinguish contractual from tortious breaches, and it applies regardless of whether the violated norm came from a treaty or from custom.

cards.q: Is state responsibility criminal or civil in character, and what follows?
cards.a: Civil and purely compensatory, not penal. It runs bilaterally between injuring and injured state, is enforced primarily by the injured state, and does not distinguish contractual from tortious breaches or treaty from customary obligations.

slides.title: Where the rules come from
slides.text: Customary international law, developed over decades out of general principles in international jurisprudence, and codified by the ILC in the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts of 2001. Their status is the point to state precisely: not formally a treaty, merely annexed to a General Assembly resolution, so the text is not binding — yet it is an extensive written statement of existing custom and is treated in practice as authoritative and often applied as though binding.

terms.def: ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts; annexed to a GA resolution, not a treaty, but treated as authoritative codification of custom.

cards.q: What is the legal status of the ILC Articles on State Responsibility?
cards.a: Not a treaty — annexed to a General Assembly resolution and not binding as such. But they codify existing customary law extensively and are applied in practice as authoritative.

slides.title: The structure and the elements
slides.text: Three parts: how responsibility arises (attribution, and possibly preclusion of wrongfulness); what its content is (the consequences for the injuring state); and how it is enforced. And the elements to prove, which is the checklist for every problem question: a breach of an international obligation, by act or omission, incompatible with the state's obligations; attributable to a state; with no circumstance precluding wrongfulness. Note the negative: fault and damage are NOT generally required — a breach suffices.

cards.q: What must be shown for state responsibility to arise?
cards.a: A breach of an international obligation by act or omission, attributable to the state, with no circumstance precluding wrongfulness. Fault and damage are not generally required.

cards.q: State A's conduct injures no one but breaches a treaty obligation. Is A responsible?
cards.a: Yes. Damage is not a general requirement of state responsibility; the breach of the obligation plus attribution suffices. Damage matters for the content of reparation, not for the existence of responsibility.

slides.title: Attribution I: the state's own organs
slides.text: A state answers only for its own acts, so everything turns on attribution. Acts of its own organs are attributable regardless of the branch of government — legislature, judiciary or executive — and regardless of the organ's position in the hierarchy. 'Organ' is read in two senses: structural, a formal state organ; and FUNCTIONAL, any person or institution empowered to exercise sovereign tasks and doing so in the case at hand. Hence outsourcing does not shed responsibility: if the state authorizes a private company to run a prison, the company's conduct is attributed to the state.

cards.q: A state contracts a private company to run a prison; the company's staff ill-treat inmates. Is the state responsible?
cards.a: Yes. Attribution covers organs in the functional sense — persons or entities empowered to exercise sovereign tasks and doing so in the case. Outsourcing a sovereign function does not shed responsibility.

cards.q: Is a state responsible for the acts of its courts, or only of its government?
cards.a: Of all branches. Conduct of the legislature, judiciary and executive is attributable regardless of the organ's position in the state's structure.

slides.title: Attribution II: private conduct
slides.text: Acts of private persons are attributable in two situations. Where the state exercises EFFECTIVE CONTROL — it prescribes the precise conduct, within a command structure; this is the Nicaragua standard, confirmed in the Bosnian Genocide case of 2007. Or where the state ACKNOWLEDGES AND ADOPTS the conduct as its own, as in the Tehran Hostages case, where a declaration of a state organ turned a private occupation into state conduct. Two further rules: insurgents' acts are attributed retroactively if they become the new government or found a new state by secession; and participation in another state's violation engages responsibility too.

terms.def: The Nicaragua standard for attributing private conduct: the state prescribes the precise conduct within a command structure.
A state adopting private conduct as its own makes it attributable — Tehran Hostages (1980).

cards.q: State A funds and arms a rebel group in State B, which then commits violations. Are those acts attributable to A?
cards.a: Only if A exercised effective control — prescribing the precise conduct within a command structure (Nicaragua; Bosnian Genocide 2007). Financing, arming and general support are not enough, though they are themselves unlawful intervention.

cards.q: Private demonstrators seize an embassy and the government publicly endorses the occupation. Attributable?
cards.a: Yes, from the moment of endorsement: a state that acknowledges and adopts private conduct as its own makes it attributable — Tehran Hostages (1980).

cards.q: When are the acts of insurgents attributed to a state?
cards.a: Retroactively, if they become the new government of the state or succeed in establishing a new state by secession.

slides.title: Circumstances precluding wrongfulness
slides.text: Injury and attribution are established, but the act is justified. Consent — voluntary, uncoerced, and only where the violated norm permits it, which is why consent cannot authorize a breach of the prohibition of force. Self-defence under Article 51, individual or collective. Countermeasures. Force majeure, where an irresistible force makes performance materially impossible — the fighter jet blown into foreign airspace by atmospheric disturbance. And necessity, from the Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros case between Hungary and Slovakia: the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril.

cards.a: Consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure and necessity — plus distress in the full ILC list. Each has its own conditions and none can justify a breach of ius cogens.

slides.title: The consequences: cessation and reparation
slides.text: Two immediate consequences: cessation, if the breach is ongoing, and assurances of non-repetition where repetition is feared. Then FULL REPARATION, in a fixed order. Restitutio in integrum — re-establishing the situation that existed before the wrongful act. Compensation where restitution is impossible: the objective market value of material damage, covering both damnum emergens, the direct loss, and lucrum cessans, the lost profit, plus interest. And satisfaction for immaterial damage, such as a mere violation of territorial integrity — a formal apology or an admission of wrongfulness.

terms.def: Re-establishing the situation that existed before the wrongful act; the primary form of reparation.
Reparation for immaterial injury — apology, acknowledgment of the breach, a declaration by a court.

cards.q: In what order do the forms of reparation apply?
cards.a: Restitution first — re-establishing the prior situation. Compensation where restitution is materially impossible, covering direct loss and lost profits with interest. Satisfaction for immaterial injury, such as an apology.

cards.q: State A briefly violates State B's airspace, causing no damage. What can B claim?
cards.a: Cessation if it continues, assurances of non-repetition if repetition is feared, and satisfaction for the immaterial injury — a formal apology or acknowledgment — since there is no material damage to compensate.

slides.title: Who may invoke responsibility, and how
slides.text: The directly injured state may — the other party to a bilateral treaty, the state whose territorial integrity was violated. And for obligations protecting collective interests, obligations ERGA OMNES, every other state to which the obligation is owed may invoke it; human rights are the example, and the inter-state complaint under the ECHR the mechanism. Enforcement is then decentralised: unilateral countermeasures, which are themselves violations of the injuring state's rights, subject to strict limits — proportionality to the original injury; no effect on fundamental human rights, ius cogens, diplomatic immunities or dispute settlement norms; no violation of third parties' rights; notification; and termination as soon as the violation ends. Where a tribunal has jurisdiction, adjudication is the alternative.

terms.def: An obligation owed to the international community as a whole, which any state to whom it is owed may invoke.

cards.q: State A commits grave human rights violations against its own population. May State C, which suffered nothing, invoke A's responsibility?
cards.a: Yes, where the obligation protects collective interests — an obligation erga omnes. Human rights are the standard example, and the inter-state complaint under the ECHR is the procedural form.

Proportionality to the original injury; no effect on fundamental human rights, ius cogens, diplomatic immunities or dispute-settlement norms; no violation of third-party rights; prior notification; and termination as soon as the wrongful act ceases.
